results.reader_title: Survey maps how European and Latin American researchers collaborate on personalised medicine
results.reader_what: A 2022 survey of EU–Latin American co-authors found missing joint funding is the main barrier to personalised-medicine collaboration.
results.reader_why: Collaboration relied mainly on home-country public grants, with little dedicated joint funding—a gap relevant to designing EU–Latin American programmes.
results.reader_more: Researchers at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid and Spain's INNOVATEC carried out the study under the EU-funded EULAC-PerMed project. They emailed 1,863 corresponding authors of 2012–2021 personalised-medicine papers co-written by EU and Latin American or Caribbean researchers; 136 replied (7.3%). Most respondents were senior university or public-institute researchers, and cancer was the leading shared field. Seventy per cent named national or regional public funding as the main source, about a third cited EU programmes, and only 5% reported funding aimed specifically at personalised medicine. Given the low response rate and corresponding-author focus, the authors present the results as a rough picture that cannot be generalised.

deep_analysis.research_question: What strategic issues, structural factors and outcomes characterise EU–Latin America and Caribbean research collaboration in personalised medicine?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Of 136 respondents, 71.65% had collaborated across the two regions in the past decade, mainly via international projects, capacity building and informal links; prior acquaintance with partners was the strongest enabling factor. Home national/regional public funding was the main source (70%), EU funding was cited by 32.5%, project grants were the dominant tool (>90%), funding targeted at personalised medicine was rare (5%), and lack of specific funding for joint actions was the leading barrier (55%).
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Literature review, then a collaboration framework, then a questionnaire validated in two EULAC-PerMed consortium workshops; online survey launched 7 June 2022 (one reminder) to 1,863 corresponding authors (1,248 EU incl. Turkey/Israel, 615 LAC) of 2,922 co-authored personalised-medicine articles from 2012–2021 (PubMed/Scopus); descriptive statistics.
deep_analysis.qualification: Low response rate (7.3%; 136 respondents), corresponding authors mainly at public institutions, descriptive statistics only; the authors say results cannot be extrapolated beyond this population.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: EU-funded evidence on how EU–CELAC research cooperation in personalised medicine is funded (national vs EU programmes) and obstructed, relevant to EU international cooperation instruments such as ICPerMed and ERA PerMed; historical context for EU–Latin America R&I cooperation.

results.reader_title: How four European chip research centres pursue greener innovation, and what drives them
results.reader_what: Four European semiconductor research organisations mainly cut cleanroom energy, water use and exhaust; funding and regulation drive their green efforts.
results.reader_why: Because these research cleanrooms serve many public and private projects, their sustainability practices affect partners' next-generation chip products.
results.reader_more: Research and technology organisations (RTOs) are non-university institutes that run shared semiconductor cleanrooms used in public and private R&D projects. VTT researchers interviewed staff at four anonymised European RTOs in two rounds in 2023–2024. Activities ranged from energy and water savings to recycling partnerships and sustainability-focused EU projects; all four named research funding as a driver, alongside regulation such as EU chemical restrictions and management pressure. One interviewee noted that SMEs often cannot meet semiconductor-industry requirements for funded consortia. With only four cases, the authors present the findings as tentative and not generalisable.

deep_analysis.research_question: What sustainability-oriented innovation (SOI) activities are European RTOs with semiconductor research infrastructure engaged in, what drives them, and who are the actors in their local green innovation ecosystems?
deep_analysis.main_finding: SOI engagement varies across the four RTOs, but all pursue operational optimisation of cleanrooms (energy, water, exhaust), while organisational-transformation and system-building activity is uneven; funding, political/regulatory pressure and top-management push are the main drivers. The authors extend Marcon et al.'s green-innovation-ecosystem actor framework with public opinion, the local municipality, distinct roles for SMEs and large firms, and the RTO as orchestrator.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Two-round qualitative study of four anonymised European RTO microelectronics departments: phone interviews plus e-mail questionnaire (Nov 2023–Jan 2024) mapped to Adams et al.'s SOI framework and verified by participants, then recorded semi-structured interviews (Jun–Jul 2024).
deep_analysis.qualification: Four anonymised cases with confidential, self-reported interview data; the authors describe the findings as tentative and not generalisable.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Evidence on Europe's semiconductor research infrastructure: how European RTO cleanrooms that host public and private R&D projects embed sustainability, how research funding and EU/national regulation drive it, and ecosystem gaps such as SME participation in funded consortia.

results.reader_title: JRC maps which advanced materials could cut critical raw material use in cars
results.reader_what: Mature alternatives can cut gallium, palladium, beryllium, magnesium and other critical materials in specific car parts; none is universal.
results.reader_why: Mature substitutes chiefly need qualification testing and pilot-line access; the findings can inform EU research programming and materials legislation.
results.reader_more: The Joint Research Centre, the European Commission's science service, prepared the study for the Commission's research directorate under its 2024 advanced-materials strategy. It compares 91 named options in seven material–application portfolios, from driver-assistance sensors and connectors to body steels, castings, thermal parts and exhaust catalysts, against the materials used today. For 62 options the lowest reported technology readiness level is 7 or higher, meaning technically mature, though not suitable everywhere. Some options create new dependencies on other materials or production capabilities, and no general replacement without platinum-group metals was found for the reference exhaust catalyst. The screening combines literature and expert judgement, without life-cycle assessment or engineering qualification.

deep_analysis.research_question: Which advanced-material options can reduce dependence on critical raw materials in selected passenger-vehicle functions, and what research and innovation is still needed?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Across seven material–application portfolios (91 named options, 62 with lowest reported TRL of 7 or above), mature options exist for specific functions (beryllium-free spring alloys, palladium-free finishes, nickel capacitor electrodes, AlN/Si3N4 substrates for BeO, silicon technologies reducing Ga/Ge in sensing, aluminium for some Mg castings, reduced Nb in selected steels), but there is no universal substitute and no general PGM-free replacement for the reference three-way catalyst. R&I needs are qualification evidence and pilot-line/test-facility access for mature options, development research for less mature ones (e.g. GeSn photonics, PGM-free catalysts), and substrate reuse and closed-loop recovery where substitution is limited.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Benchmark-relative screening of options for the same vehicle function against six criteria (CRM reduction, performance, lifetime/reliability, cost, circularity, environmental sustainability), with a CRM-reduction mechanism taxonomy, technology readiness levels and separate flags for new material or capability dependencies; published evidence plus expert judgement.
deep_analysis.qualification: Screening assessment based on published evidence and expert judgement, without life-cycle assessment or engineering qualification; excludes traction batteries, drive motors and fuel cells; TRL 7+ signals maturity, not suitability for every vehicle application.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Direct EU R&I policy input prepared by the JRC for DG RTD under Action 3 of COM(2024) 98, noting EU capability strengths (steel, aluminium casting, connector plating, catalysts), import dependencies (alloying inputs, primary magnesium, PGMs) and gaps between research strength and manufacturing capability.

results.reader_title: Did announcing the EU AI Act slow AI medical-device innovation? Early data say no
results.reader_what: AI medical-device approvals and patent filings showed no sustained significant change after the EU AI Act's 2021 announcement.
results.reader_why: It counters claims that the Act's announcement itself slowed EU market access, though effects of actual implementation remain untested.
results.reader_more: Researchers at the Technical University of Munich applied interrupted time-series analysis, which compares trends before and after an event, to data from April 2019 to April 2025. They tracked US FDA approvals of AI devices from EU makers, the Health AI Register of certified devices in the EU, and WIPO patent filings. Approvals of EU-made devices jumped once around the announcement but did not keep rising faster. OECD venture-capital figures rose more in the EU than elsewhere, but only three data points per period allowed descriptive comparison. The study examines the announcement, not the Act's later obligations.

deep_analysis.work_kind: Quasi-experimental empirical study (interrupted time-series); journal article labelled 'Review'
deep_analysis.research_question: How did the April 2021 announcement of the EU AI Act influence market access and the pace of innovation for AI-enabled medical devices and healthcare products in the EU?
deep_analysis.main_finding: No sustained, statistically significant post-announcement change in EU-origin FDA approvals, Health AI Register device counts or WIPO AI patent filings; EU-origin FDA approvals showed a one-off level increase (beta2 about 2.0, p = 0.014) without a trend change. OECD/Preqin venture data showed larger descriptive increases for the EU27 (deals +117%, volume +146%) than other regions, with too few observations for inference.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Interrupted time-series analysis (OLS with Newey-West errors, 24-month lag) on monthly data April 2019–April 2025 from the FDA AI-enabled device list (121 devices from 14 EU countries), the Health AI Register and WIPO PATENTSCOPE; exploratory comparison (Welch's t-test) of annual OECD AI Policy Observatory venture data 2018–2024.
deep_analysis.qualification: Tests association with the Act's announcement, not its later implementation; proxies (FDA approvals of EU-made devices, registry counts, patents) are indirect, confounders such as COVID-19 are acknowledged, and the venture-capital comparison is descriptive only.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Early quantitative evidence on whether EU AI regulation dampened European health-AI innovation and market access, relevant to the recurring regulation-versus-innovation debate in EU R&I policy; historical baseline for later implementation effects.

claims.qualification: Tests association with the Act's announcement, not its later implementation; proxies (FDA approvals of EU-made devices, registry counts, patents) are indirect, confounders such as COVID-19 are acknowledged, and the venture-capital comparison is descriptive only.
claims.text: An interrupted time-series analysis found no sustained significant change in approvals or patent filings for AI-enabled medical devices after the EU AI Act's April 2021 announcement.

results.reader_title: EU health research funding shifted toward applied, population-level work more than resulting publications did
results.reader_what: EU collaborative health projects moved toward population, diagnostic and health-system research since 2008, but their publications changed only moderately.
results.reader_why: Suggests EU funding priorities reshape funded project portfolios more readily than the scientific knowledge those projects produce.
results.reader_more: KU Leuven researchers used large-scale text analysis and supervised classification to sort project descriptions and resulting publications by research level, from basic biomedical science to patient-, population- and health-system-oriented work. They compared EU Framework Programme collaborative health research (FP7 and Horizon 2020) and European Research Council life-science grants with US National Institutes of Health collaborative programmes. The EU collaborative projects shifted markedly, while ERC grants and NIH's P01 and U01 programmes stayed more stable and dominated by basic research. Basic biomedical research remained central in publications even from EU collaborative projects. The authors conclude that funders' expectations change more than realised research trajectories.

deep_analysis.research_question: To what extent have shifts in public funding priorities toward higher-level, patient-oriented health research been implemented in EU and NIH collaborative funding portfolios and reflected in their scientific outputs since 2008?

At publication level changes were more moderate, with basic biomedical research remaining central even in FP-HR outputs, a partial translation of funding priorities.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Large-scale text analysis and supervised classification of research level in project descriptions and linked publications for EU FP-HR, ERC Life Sciences and NIH P01, U01 and UM1 funding since 2008.
deep_analysis.qualification: Research levels are inferred by automated text classification of project descriptions and publications; associations, not causal effects of funding policy; the authors stress enduring epistemic and institutional constraints on outputs.

They draw lessons from three historical aviation transitions, build a two-by-two scenario matrix from AI integration and institutional adaptability, and refine it with a three-round Delphi, in which 16 senior experts rated and revised the scenarios. The four futures are Strategic Co-evolution, Human-Centric Continuity, Latent Obsolescence and Human Displacement; experts judged the first most plausible and desirable. The authors note the small panel, researcher judgement in choosing the axes, and a purely qualitative design.

deep_analysis.research_question: How might AI integration reshape human roles in aviation, and how can a co-evolutionary foresight framework structure plausible futures?

deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Three-layer design: historical case analysis of three aviation transitions, theory-informed 2x2 scenario construction (evolutionary economics, socio-technical systems theory) and a three-round Delphi with 16 senior aviation stakeholders, building on a systematic literature review (2000–2025).

admission.reason: Reviews Armenia's reforms to bring its science system closer to the European Research Area and European higher-education standards, and benchmarks almost 4,000 Armenian scientists against Italy using the Fractional Scientific Strength indicator; a substantive study of research-system convergence on the ERA's periphery. Historical context.

results.reader_title: Benchmark against Italy shows Armenia's research system still lags despite reforms toward Europe
results.reader_what: Only 28.3% of Armenian scholars published a Web of Science article in 2017–2021, versus over 98% of Italian academics.
results.reader_why: Field-level strengths and gaps give Armenian policymakers evidence for reforms aimed at closer integration with the European Research Area.
results.reader_more: Italian and Armenian researchers first review Armenia's post-Soviet reforms, including a new Higher Education and Science Committee, plans to move research institutes into universities, and publication thresholds for basic funding from 2026. They then apply Fractional Scientific Strength, a field-normalised productivity indicator developed by the Italian co-authors, to 2017–2021 Web of Science data for almost 4,000 Armenian scientists. Armenia lags Italy overall and has a much weaker presence in high-impact journals, though a few fields, such as integrative medicine and energy and fuels, come closer. The analysis relies on indexed journal output only.

deep_analysis.research_question: How does the research performance of Armenian scientists compare with Italian benchmarks after reforms intended to integrate Armenia's science system with the European Research Area?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Armenia lags Italy in research productivity and impact: only 28.3% of Armenian scholars published at least one WoS-indexed article in 2017–2021 versus over 98% of Italian academics, with a much weaker presence in high-impact journals; relative performance varies by field, with some (e.g. integrative and complementary medicine, energy and fuels) closer to Italian levels.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Review of Armenian science and higher-education reforms, then Fractional Scientific Strength (FSS) productivity measurement of almost 4,000 Armenian scientists on 2017–2021 Web of Science data, aggregated to field, institution and national level and benchmarked against Italian academics.
deep_analysis.qualification: Bibliometric indicators capture only Web of Science-indexed journal output; Italy is a single benchmark country; findings describe 2017–2021 performance, not the effects of the latest reforms.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Evidence on research-system convergence at the edge of the ERA: how a post-Soviet partner country's reforms toward European standards translate, or not, into research performance relative to an EU member state.
